subtopics.name: Care of clients with sensory impairment

questions.stem: An 83-year-old client with heart failure and chronic kidney disease takes digoxin 0.25 mg daily and furosemide 80 mg daily. The client reports nausea, poor appetite and seeing yellow-green halos around lights. Apical pulse is 46/min and irregular. Labs: potassium 3.0 mEq/L, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL and digoxin level 3.1 ng/mL (therapeutic 0.5 to 2.0). Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Hold the digoxin and notify the provider
Place the client on continuous cardiac monitoring
Give the next dose with food to ease the nausea
Give an extra dose of furosemide to remove the drug
Tell the client the halos will clear with new glasses

parameters.text: Fingerstick blood glucose before meals and at bedtime
Body weight measured once a week on the same scale
Pupil size and reaction to light each shift

rationale.correct: Digoxin toxicity is more likely with older age, kidney disease and low potassium; hold the drug, monitor the heart, correct potassium and consider digoxin immune fab.

perOption.c1: GI symptoms, visual changes, bradycardia and a high level, worsened by low potassium and kidney disease, show digoxin toxicity.
perOption.c2: Nausea alone does not explain the visual changes, bradycardia and drug level.
perOption.c3: Heart failure does not cause yellow-green halos and a high digoxin level.
perOption.a1: Stopping the drug is the first step.
perOption.a4: Furosemide lowers potassium further, worsening toxicity.
perOption.a5: The visual changes are from toxicity.
perOption.p1: Shows dysrhythmias and response to treatment.
perOption.p2: Low potassium worsens toxicity; levels guide treatment, including digoxin immune fab.
perOption.p3: Not a guide to digoxin toxicity.
perOption.p4: Not frequent enough to guide this emergency.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes received insulin lispro 12 units before a breakfast tray that was then sent back untouched because of nausea. An hour later the client is found sweating, confused and unable to follow commands. The fingerstick glucose is 36 mg/dL. An IV line is in place. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Give IV 50% dextrose as prescribed by protocol
Recheck the glucose 15 minutes after treatment
Give 4 oz of orange juice by mouth
Give the next scheduled insulin dose early
Wait 30 minutes to see whether the client improves

parameters.text: Body weight measured once a week
Bowel sounds in each of the four quadrants

rationale.correct: Severe hypoglycemia with altered consciousness: IV dextrose or IM glucagon, recheck in 15 minutes, then food when safe; review why the insulin was not matched to intake.

perOption.c1: A glucose of 36 mg/dL with confusion after rapid-acting insulin without food is severe hypoglycemia.
perOption.c3: The low glucose explains the confusion and must be corrected first.
perOption.a1: IV dextrose corrects glucose fastest in a client who cannot swallow safely.
perOption.a2: Rechecking confirms the response and guides further treatment.
perOption.a3: A confused client who cannot follow commands may aspirate.
perOption.a5: Delay can cause seizures and brain injury.
perOption.p3: Not the key guide in hypoglycemia.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
American Diabetes Association Standards of Care

questions.stem: A client who weighs 82 kg and has normal kidney function is prescribed IV vancomycin 15 mg/kg every 12 hours for MRSA bacteremia. The pharmacy sends vials reconstituted to a concentration of 50 mg/mL, and the nurse will add the dose to a 250 mL bag. How many milliliters of the reconstituted solution contain the dose? Round to one decimal place.

rationale.correct: Dose: 15 mg x 82 kg = 1,230 mg. Volume: 1,230 mg / 50 mg/mL = 24.6 mL.
references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A 64-year-old client with hypothyroidism whose TSH remains high on the current dose is prescribed levothyroxine 0.075 mg by mouth each morning. The pharmacy stocks only 25 mcg tablets. The client asks how many tablets to take each morning until the new strength arrives. How many tablets should the nurse give?

rationale.correct: 0.075 mg = 75 mcg. 75 mcg / 25 mcg per tablet = 3 tablets.
references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A nurse on a medical unit is planning laboratory monitoring for four clients who each take a medication with a narrow safety margin or a serious interaction risk. For each medication, indicate the laboratory value the nurse should check most closely.

rationale.correct: Match drugs to their monitoring: warfarin (INR), heparin (aPTT or anti-Xa), lithium (drug level) and digoxin with diuretics (potassium, plus levels).

perOption.r1:c3: Warfarin levels are not routinely measured.
perOption.r2:c2: aPTT or anti-Xa guides heparin dosing.
perOption.r3:c3: Lithium levels guide dosing and detect toxicity.
perOption.r4:c3: Digoxin levels matter too, but low potassium from furosemide is the key risk to monitor.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges

questions.stem: Facility policy requires an independent double check by a second nurse for certain high-alert medications. Which medications usually require this check? Select all that apply.

options.text: A continuous IV heparin infusion
IV insulin for diabetic ketoacidosis
Oral acetaminophen 650 mg for a headache
A PCA syringe of hydromorphone
Oral docusate 100 mg as a stool softener
IV chemotherapy

rationale.correct: High-alert drugs (insulin, heparin, opioids, chemotherapy, concentrated electrolytes) often need independent double checks.

perOption.d: IV opioids in PCA are high-alert.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: The nurse is giving IV push furosemide through a saline lock. Place the steps in order.

items.text: Flush with saline at the same rate, then check the client's response
Check the client's identity with two identifiers and scan the medication
Push the furosemide slowly over the recommended time
Clean the port and flush with saline to check the line is patent

rationale.correct: IV push: identify, scan, clean the port, flush to check patency, give slowly, flush at the same rate and assess.

perOption.a: Identity and drug checks come first.
perOption.d: Clears the line and evaluates the effect.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: At 0900 the nurse reviews assessment data before giving scheduled medications. Highlight the medications that should be held and reported.

rationale.correct: Check vital signs and labs before cardiac drugs: hold beta-blockers for bradycardia, ACE inhibitors for hypotension and digoxin for low potassium, and report.

perOption.r1: Bradycardia with symptoms is a reason to hold a beta-blocker.
perOption.r2: Hypotension is a reason to hold an ACE inhibitor.
perOption.r3: Low potassium raises the risk of digoxin toxicity.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client has been receiving clindamycin for 6 days for a skin infection. The client now has six watery stools a day, abdominal cramps and a temperature of 38.2 °C (100.8 °F). What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the prescribed loperamide and encourage fluids
Start contact precautions and report so C. difficile testing can be done
Tell the client the diarrhea is an expected side effect that will stop when the course ends
Give a probiotic yogurt with lunch and continue to watch the number of stools

rationale.correct: New watery diarrhea during antibiotics suggests C. difficile: contact precautions, soap-and-water hand hygiene, testing and avoiding antidiarrheals.

perOption.a: Antidiarrheals can worsen C. difficile infection.
perOption.b: Antibiotic-associated watery diarrhea with fever suggests C. difficile; isolation and testing come first.
perOption.d: This does not address a possible C. difficile infection.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes controlled on metformin starts high-dose prednisone for a COPD flare. On day 2, afternoon glucose readings are 280 to 340 mg/dL, while morning readings are about 140 mg/dL. What should the nurse expect?

options.text: Stopping the prednisone because it is causing the high afternoon glucose readings
Insulin such as NPH timed to the steroid's afternoon peak effect
No change, since steroid-related high glucose is harmless
Doubling the metformin dose immediately to bring the glucose down

rationale.correct: Steroids cause hyperglycemia that peaks in the afternoon after morning doses; it is managed with insulin timed to the steroid while the steroid continues.

perOption.a: The steroid is needed for the COPD flare; glucose is managed instead.
perOption.b: Morning prednisone raises glucose most in the afternoon and evening; insulin is timed to match.
perOption.c: High glucose increases infection risk and can cause dehydration.
perOption.d: Metformin changes are slow and may not control steroid-induced hyperglycemia.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
American Diabetes Association Standards of Care

questions.stem: A client receiving enoxaparin 40 mg daily for clot prevention after abdominal surgery has a platelet count that fell from 245,000/mm3 before surgery to 98,000/mm3 on day 8. There is no bleeding. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the dose as scheduled, since there is no bleeding
Hold the enoxaparin and report the platelet drop to the provider
Switch the client to IV heparin, since it does not affect platelets
Give a platelet transfusion to bring the count back up

rationale.correct: A platelet fall of more than 50% 5 to 10 days into heparin or enoxaparin suggests HIT; hold all heparin and report.

perOption.a: A drop of more than 50% 5 to 10 days into heparin therapy suggests heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
perOption.b: Low-molecular-weight heparin can cause HIT; the drug is held and the provider evaluates.
perOption.c: Unfractionated heparin causes HIT even more often.
perOption.d: Platelet transfusions can worsen clotting in HIT.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: For each medication, choose the adverse effect the client should be taught to report.

options.text: Unexplained muscle pain or weakness
Dry cough
Ankle swelling
Orange urine
Swelling of the ankles
Black tongue
Swelling of the lips or tongue
Increased appetite
Hair growth
Weight gain
Muscle pain with rapid breathing and weakness
Low blood pressure

rationale.correct: Teach the key adverse effect for each drug: statin myopathy, amlodipine edema, ACE inhibitor angioedema and metformin lactic acidosis.

perOption.b2:b: A common effect of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers.
perOption.b3:a: Angioedema is a serious ACE inhibitor reaction.
perOption.b4:a: Metformin is weight-neutral or causes loss.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client receives high-dose IV methotrexate for osteosarcoma. A prescription for leucovorin is due to start 24 hours after the methotrexate. Why is the timing of leucovorin so important?

options.text: Leucovorin makes methotrexate kill more cancer cells, so it is given late for full effect
It rescues normal cells from methotrexate, so a late dose risks severe toxicity
Leucovorin is an antiemetic that is given if the client starts to vomit
Leucovorin replaces potassium lost in the urine during methotrexate therapy

rationale.correct: High-dose methotrexate requires leucovorin rescue on schedule, plus hydration, urine alkalinization and methotrexate levels.

perOption.a: Leucovorin protects normal cells, not the cancer.
perOption.b: Leucovorin rescue must start on time to prevent bone marrow suppression, mucositis and kidney damage.
perOption.d: It is not an electrolyte replacement.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: For each client, indicate the most appropriate diet.

rows.text: A client with heart failure and ankle edema
A client the day before a colonoscopy
A client with chronic kidney disease not on dialysis and a potassium of 5.6 mEq/L
A client with chronic constipation and diverticulosis without inflammation

rationale.correct: Match diets to conditions: low sodium for heart failure, clear liquids before colonoscopy, low potassium and phosphorus in CKD and high fiber for constipation and diverticulosis.

perOption.r2:c2: Clear liquids are used during bowel preparation.
perOption.r3:c1: Sodium may be limited, but potassium and phosphorus are key.
perOption.r3:c3: Kidney disease with high potassium needs these limits.
perOption.r3:c4: High-fiber foods can be high in potassium.
perOption.r4:c4: Fiber prevents constipation and diverticular problems.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client receiving continuous nasogastric feeding at 65 mL/hr vomits a moderate amount of formula and has a distended abdomen. The head of the bed is at 35 degrees. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Increase the head of the bed to 60 degrees and continue the feeding at the same rate
Stop the feeding, check the client's breathing and notify the provider
Slow the feeding to 30 mL/hr and recheck in 4 hours
Flush the tube with 60 mL of water to clear it

rationale.correct: With vomiting or distention during tube feeding, stop the feeding, assess for aspiration and notify the provider.

perOption.a: Positioning helps, but feeding must stop when the client vomits.
perOption.b: Vomiting with distention means intolerance and aspiration risk; the feeding is paused and the airway assessed.
perOption.c: Continuing the feeding after vomiting risks aspiration.
perOption.d: Adding fluid to a distended stomach worsens the problem.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is providing care after a client's expected death. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place the body flat with a pillow under the head
Remove tubes and lines unless an autopsy or coroner case requires them to stay
Offer the family time alone with the body
Close the eyes and replace dentures if possible
Take the client's jewelry home with the nurse for safekeeping
Leave the body uncleaned until the funeral home arrives

rationale.correct: Postmortem care: position flat with a pillow, close eyes, replace dentures, clean the body, remove lines per policy, secure valuables and support the family.

perOption.a: Prevents blood pooling in the face.
perOption.e: Valuables are documented and given to family or secured per policy.
perOption.f: The body is cleaned and positioned with dignity.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old client with advanced dementia and a hip fracture does not ask for pain medicine. The client grimaces and moans when turned and has an as-needed oxycodone prescription. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Wait until the client asks for pain medicine before giving any
Use a behavioral pain scale and ask about scheduled analgesia
Avoid opioids completely because they cause confusion in older adults
Turn the client less often so that the hip pain is not triggered as much

rationale.correct: Clients who cannot self-report need behavioral pain scales and often scheduled analgesia, especially before care that causes pain.

perOption.a: Clients with advanced dementia often cannot ask for analgesia.
perOption.b: Behavioral tools detect pain, and scheduled analgesics prevent untreated pain in clients who cannot request them.
perOption.c: Untreated pain can also cause delirium; careful opioid use is appropriate.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: The nurse is helping a client who can bear weight on both legs move from the bed to a chair. Place the steps in order.

items.text: Apply a gait belt around the client's waist
Lock the bed wheels and place the chair at the bedside at a slight angle
Help the client stand, pivot and sit in the chair
Help the client sit on the edge of the bed and dangle the legs

rationale.correct: Bed-to-chair transfer: lock the bed, position the chair, dangle, apply a gait belt, stand, pivot and sit.

perOption.a: Prevents the bed and chair from moving.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client had an indwelling urinary catheter placed for surgery 3 days ago and is now walking and voiding sensations are present. The unit has a nurse-driven catheter removal protocol. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Leave the catheter in until discharge to avoid the risk of retention
Check whether it is still needed and remove it per the unit protocol
Ask the client whether they would like to keep the catheter for comfort
Change the catheter to a larger size to prevent any leaking around it

rationale.correct: Review catheter need daily and remove it promptly when no longer indicated; nurse-driven protocols reduce CAUTI.

perOption.a: Each extra day of catheter use raises infection risk.
perOption.b: Daily review and prompt removal under nurse-driven protocols reduce CAUTI.
perOption.c: Comfort alone is not an indication for a catheter.
perOption.d: There is no indication described for continuing the catheter.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old client in long-term care has been taking oxycodone after a fall. Highlight the findings that suggest constipation or impaction.

segments.text: last bowel movement was 5 days ago
Small amounts of liquid stool are leaking

rationale.correct: Signs of constipation and impaction include no stool for several days, bloating, reduced appetite and leaking liquid stool.

perOption.s2: A long interval without stool suggests constipation.
perOption.s4: Fullness and bloating suggest retained stool.
perOption.s6: Liquid stool leaking around a hard mass suggests impaction.
perOption.s10: Constipation often lowers appetite in older adults.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client with right-sided hemiplegia after a stroke is at risk for contractures. Which nursing action best prevents them?

options.text: Keep the right arm in a sling across the chest through the day and night
Do passive range of motion on the right arm and leg several times a day
Keep the client on bed rest until strength returns to the right side
Avoid touching the right side so the client is not uncomfortable

rationale.correct: Prevent contractures with passive range of motion, good positioning and splints as prescribed.

perOption.b: Passive range of motion keeps joints mobile and prevents contractures.
perOption.d: Avoiding the weak side increases contracture risk.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client in the last days of life becomes restless, pulls at the bedsheets and moans. The client has not voided for 10 hours, and the last pain medication was 6 hours ago. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Give the prescribed as-needed haloperidol for terminal agitation
Check for a distended bladder and assess for pain
Ask the family to leave the room so the client can rest
Raise the bed rails and dim the lights

rationale.correct: Before treating terminal restlessness with drugs, check for reversible causes such as a full bladder, pain, constipation and hypoxia.

perOption.a: Medication may be needed, but reversible causes such as urinary retention and pain come first.
perOption.b: Urinary retention and pain are common, reversible causes of restlessness near death.
perOption.c: Family presence often comforts; the cause must be found.
perOption.d: This does not address the likely causes.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.educationalObjective: Assess restlessness at the end of life.

questions.stem: A client's hearing aid whistles when it is placed in the ear. What should the nurse check first?

options.text: Whether it is fully inserted and the canal is free of wax
Whether the volume is set as high as it will go
Whether the battery should be soaked in water
Whether the client needs a new prescription for glasses

rationale.correct: Hearing aid feedback usually means poor fit or wax; check placement, clean the aid and canal and adjust volume.

perOption.a: Whistling usually means the aid is not seated well or wax is blocking the canal.
perOption.b: High volume causes whistling; it does not fix it.
perOption.c: Batteries and aids must be kept dry.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with paranoid personality disorder refuses a new medication and says, "Why are you changing it? What are you trying to do to me?" What is the nurse's best approach?

options.text: Tell the client the medication is harmless and they should trust the staff
Explain honestly what the medication is and why it was prescribed
Hide the medication in food so the client takes it without arguing
Joke gently about the client's suspicion to lighten the mood a little

rationale.correct: With paranoid clients, be honest, clear, consistent and businesslike; avoid hidden actions or humor that may be misread.

perOption.a: Asking for trust does not reduce suspicion.
perOption.b: Clients with paranoid traits respond best to clear, honest, consistent explanations.
perOption.c: Covert administration is unethical and destroys trust.
perOption.d: Humor can be misread as mockery.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Communicate with a client who has paranoid traits.

questions.stem: The spouse of a client with moderate Alzheimer's disease says, "I haven't slept a full night in months and I snapped at them yesterday. I feel terrible." Which intervention should the nurse suggest first?

options.text: Encourage the spouse to try harder to stay patient with the client
Help the spouse find respite care and a caregiver support group
Suggest the spouse give the client a sleeping pill each night
Tell the spouse that placement in a facility is the best solution now

rationale.correct: Recognize caregiver strain and offer respite, support groups and community resources.

perOption.a: This adds guilt and does not address exhaustion.
perOption.b: Caregiver strain is reduced by respite and support; exhaustion raises the risk of neglect or harm.
perOption.c: Sedatives raise fall and confusion risk in dementia.
perOption.d: Many options exist; respite and support come first.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
